name: Priya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at the Millbrook depot by half six, and I run a four-person distribution crew, so the low and medium voltage lines that feed houses and farms up in the hills. Most days it's pole changes, fixing sagging spans, swapping out old transformers, and when the weather turns it's storm work until the job's done, sometimes eighteen hours straight. My truck's number 41, an old bucket truck with a hydraulic leak we keep patching.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment you close the switch and a whole valley lights back up, and you hear a dog barking because the farmhouse heater kicked on. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, because this company pays less than the big outfits down on the coast, and there's no other line depot within ninety minutes, so they know we're stuck. That, and the new tablet app they want us to log everything on. I still fill in the paper job pack and let Dev type it up.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dev's the oldest guy on my crew, fifty-six, and he taught me half of what I know before they made me foreperson over him. He laughs about it. He's also our union steward's right hand, and I'm the steward, so we spend a lot of lunch breaks in the truck arguing about overtime rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly. At the depot I'd say the robots aren't climbing poles in an ice storm, and the company should stop buying gadgets and start paying people. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about how the money spent on AI should have gone into wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I don't want to learn another system, and I'm not good with screens, I'll admit that. If it all fizzles, my job stays my job, and the fight stays the same old fight about pay and staffing, which at least I know how to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes, so I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep pushing in the next pay round, which is in March, for the gap with the coast to close, and I'd keep refusing to put my crew's hours through the tablet until they fix the bugs. Maybe I'd finally get the clutch on my car paid off by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be relieved. Is there anything about AI you'd miss if it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Tomas, my partner, uses a chatbot to write his shift swap messages at the care home, and he says it's handy. I've never touched one. I'd rather ring someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you be paying off first in a normal year like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, because that car is how I get up to the depot before the first bus even runs. After that it'd be a few hundred put aside, which I've never managed. Right now if the fridge died I'd be borrowing from Tomas's mum.

S0.say: I'd tell people the robots aren't climbing poles in an ice storm. The company should stop buying gadgets and pay its crews properly.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I don't want to learn another system and I'm not good with screens. If it fizzles, my job stays my job and the old fight about pay carries on.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and pushes in the March pay round to close the wage gap with coastal companies. Pays off her car loan by summer and keeps logging work on paper.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of smugness that the hype didn't land.
S0.quote: At the depot I'd say the robots aren't climbing poles in an ice storm, and the company should stop buying gadgets and start paying people.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is a proud, hands-on crew leader who sees technology mostly as a distraction from the real issue, which is pay. She admits plainly that screens aren't her strength. Her savings are so thin that a broken fridge means borrowing from her partner's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in writing that no crew gets cut because a drone does the patrols. Line patrol is what the young ones learn on, walking the route and spotting the cracked insulators. If the drone does it, where do they learn? I'd say that loud at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd let on. I'm good at what I do, but I'm bad at learning new tools, and if the job turns into half climbing and half staring at a screen of drone photos, the people who'll do well are the ones like the twenty-two-year-olds who grew up on phones. I could end up being the foreperson who slows things down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to open talks before anything is rolled out, not after, and I'd want a no-cuts clause for at least three years. I'd also try to put fifty a week aside, which means no more takeaway on Fridays. And I suppose I'd let Dev show me the drone software, slowly, though I'd hate every minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a storm on the forecast but it hasn't reached the ridge yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, my apprentice. He's nineteen and he's still at the stage where patrol work and grunt work is how you build up your eye. If the company decides it only needs trained climbers and drone operators, apprentices like him are the first line they cut from the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate learning the drone software, but you'd do it. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I don't, someone else signs off my crew's work and I lose the say over who goes up the pole. That's a safety thing for me, not a pride thing. I've seen what happens when the person deciding has never stood in the bucket.

S1.say: I'd say at work and at the union meeting that no crew gets cut because a drone does the patrols. If machines walk the routes, where do the apprentices learn?
S1.think: It scares me more than I'd let on, because I'm good at the job but bad at learning new tools. I could end up being the foreperson who slows everyone down.
S1.do: Gets the union to open talks before any rollout and push for a three-year no-cuts clause. Starts saving about fifty a week by dropping Friday takeaways, and lets Dev teach her the drone software.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm on the forecast that hasn't reached the ridge yet.
S1.quote: I could end up being the foreperson who slows things down.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is all about protecting apprentices and crews, while privately the fear is about herself falling behind. She'd learn the software only to keep control over safety decisions, which says a lot about what she values. The union is her first tool, not retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, before the companies decide everything. I'd be at every meeting saying the grid is public infrastructure and nobody should be allowed to swap out a whole workforce in two years. I'd probably even post, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished in this job. Not straight away, because getting a robot up a wet pole in the hills is harder than in a warehouse, but in two years the company would be testing them on the easy straight runs, and I'd be told my crew is down to two. I've got no savings, there's no other depot near Millbrook, and I can't see myself sitting in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to the union regional office and demand an emergency meeting about job guarantees and pay protection. I'd cut everything I can, the phone plan, the gym I never go to, and I'd move my car payments to the smallest amount the bank would allow. I'd write to our local representative every week, and I'd ask Tomas if we could move in with his mum for a bit to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight just thinking about telling the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the crew that morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand by truck 41 and say I don't know what's coming, but I'm not going to lie to you. Then I'd tell them to come to the meeting on Thursday, every single one of them, including Kofi. Dev would make a joke about robots needing a steward too, and I'd love him for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what's the thing you'd most want to have that you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money in the bank, plain and simple. If I had six months saved I could fight properly without panicking about rent. With two years I can't save my way out of anything on what they pay us.

S2.say: The government has to step in now, because the grid is public infrastructure. Nobody should be allowed to swap out a whole workforce in two years.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished in this job, with robots tested on the easy runs and my crew cut to two. I've got no savings, no other depot nearby, and I can't see myself in an office.
S2.do: Demands an emergency union meeting on job guarantees within the first month and cuts her phone plan, gym and car payments. Writes weekly to her local representative and asks her partner about moving in with his mother to save rent.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a tight chest at the thought of telling her crew.
S2.quote: I'd stand by truck 41 and say I don't know what's coming, but I'm not going to lie to you.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version flips her from a calm sceptic into someone who would organise hard. Her thin savings are the core of the fear: she says two years isn't enough to save her way out of anything. Even so, her first thought is her crew, not herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say the public has to own this change, not the shareholders. But with five years I'd add that there's no excuse now. If the company and the government can see it coming and still don't plan for the crews, that's a choice, and I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years doesn't help me as much as people think. It's five years of watching it come, and I'm not someone who'll suddenly enjoy retraining. I'd be thirty-two, still renting, still on the low pay scale, and I'd be the experienced one they'd keep longest and then let go last, which somehow feels worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to get a proper agreement: retraining paid by the company, on company time, and a guaranteed job somewhere in the grid for anyone with ten years in. I'd get myself on the union's regional committee so I'm in the room. And I'd try hard to build up two months of savings, which means I'd take every bit of storm overtime going, even the miserable night shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, just slower. Like a long drip instead of a burst pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the extra time doesn't help you much. Is there anything it does change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the fight. With two years you're just grabbing what you can. With five you can actually write rules, like a robot can't work live lines without a qualified human signing off, and that keeps people like me needed for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas about your plans together, if this were coming by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about getting a dog and a place with a yard. I'd tell him let's wait on the place, but we're getting the dog, because I'm not putting my whole life on hold for a robot.

S3.say: The public has to own this change, not the shareholders. With five years of warning there's no excuse, and failing to plan for the crews is a choice.
S3.think: Five years doesn't help me as much as people think, because I won't suddenly enjoy retraining. I'd be thirty-two, still renting on low pay, kept longest and let go last.
S3.do: Pushes in year one for paid retraining on company time and a guaranteed grid job for staff with ten years in. Joins the union's regional committee and takes every storm overtime shift to build two months of savings.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, but slower, like a long drip instead of a burst pipe.
S3.quote: We're getting the dog, because I'm not putting my whole life on hold for a robot.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't calm her, it just changes the shape of her fight from grabbing to writing rules. She sees a human sign-off rule for live-line work as her best protection. The dog line showed a stubborn streak that runs right through her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say we've got time to do this right, so let's do it right. That means training funds, public ownership of the new equipment, and nobody thrown away. I'd say it calmly, which isn't my normal style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the first one where I can picture getting through. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd have had time to fight for rules and maybe to become the person who inspects what the robots do, because somebody has to know what a bad splice looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd push the union to get a training fund into the next contract, paid into every month, so it's there when we need it. I'd put my name down for the safety inspector course the union runs, even though it's classroom work and I hate classrooms. And I'd keep going on the crew, because that's still the job for years yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I feel like I'd still have my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you hate classrooms. What would make that course bearable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was taught by someone who's done the work, not some trainer reading slides. And if Dev did it with me. We'd sit at the back and pass notes like kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years change things for you compared with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd be fighting for scraps. With five I'd be writing rules while it's already starting. With ten I can actually build something for the next lot, like Kofi, so they're not as stuck as I'd be.

S4.say: We've got ten years to do this right, so let's do it right. That means training funds, public ownership of the new equipment, and nobody thrown away.
S4.think: Ten years is the first picture where I can see myself getting through, maybe as the person who inspects what the robots do. Somebody has to know what a bad splice looks like.
S4.do: Pushes for a monthly training fund in the next union contract and signs up for the union's safety inspector course. Keeps working on her crew, expecting the job to last for years yet.
S4.feel: Anxious but steady, with her hands still on the wheel.
S4.quote: Somebody has to know what a bad splice looks like.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is the only picture where she talks about her own future instead of just defending what exists. She'd accept classroom training if it's taught by people from the trade and Dev comes along. Her thoughts keep returning to the apprentice, Kofi.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years with no savings, no other depot, and a job I've given my twenties to. What would help is a law that says grid companies can't cut crews without retraining and a job guarantee, and honestly, being paid what the coast pays so I'd have something saved before any of it starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who keeps the lights on while all this happens. Every one of those robots and data centres needs power, and it's people like me in the rain at three in the morning making that happen. The people building this future should remember that the grid is held up by hands.

headlineQuote: The people building this future should remember that the grid is held up by hands.
portrait: Priya Silva is a 27-year-old foreperson who runs a four-person distribution crew out of a hill-country depot, the only one within ninety minutes. She's the union steward, proud of her skill, low paid compared with coastal companies, and has almost nothing saved. She avoids screens and never uses AI, so the slow scenarios make her uneasy about falling behind, while the fast AGI picture alarms her. Her answer to every scenario is to organise: talks, rules, training funds and job guarantees. Only with ten years of warning can she picture a future for herself, inspecting the robots' work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years with no savings, no other depot nearby and a job she has given her twenties to leaves her nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping grid companies from cutting crews without retraining and a job guarantee, plus pay that matches the coastal companies so she could build savings first.
